meta.note: The co-op study (Prairie Valley Co-op, its 112 irrigation pumps, its tariff and every number about them) is fictional and illustrative: no dataset was simulated or measured, so its results (6.2, 4.6, 4.3 and 4.1 kW, the intervals) are assumed example outputs, not computed. The reader's own study is their research capstone (CR). intro: Twelve tasks: seven marked at once, on a fictional co-op study; five texts on your own study, which you rate against stated points.
No hints. Part A works on the co-op proposal above; parts B to D on your research capstone, with work outside this page.
Task 1 first: the seven marked tasks open once your review of the co-op proposal is submitted. Each written text then stays as you submitted it.
Your answers and times stay in this browser. At the end, “Copy my results” gives a plain-text summary, with what you typed, for a mentor.

wait.question: This task opens once task 1, your review of the co-op proposal, is submitted.
wait.why: Task 1 first. The marked tasks name concerns about the co-op proposal, so your review finds its own before you see them. Tasks 6, 7, 8 and 12, on your own study, are open now.

study.title: Did a night-pumping tariff move irrigation out of the co-op's peak?
study.who: A graduate student's proposal, with a first result, for the board of Prairie Valley Co-op.
fields: Did Prairie Valley Co-op's 2024 night-pumping tariff lower irrigation peak demand?
The co-op's board, which votes in 2026 on keeping the tariff.
Cheaper energy from 22:00 to 06:00 and a higher price from 14:00 to 20:00 on summer weekdays. Each farm chose whether to join.
Hourly meter readings of the co-op's 112 irrigation pumps, summers 2020 to 2024.
[[difference-in-differences|Difference-in-differences]]: the 41 pumps that joined in 2024 against the 71 that did not, before and after.
Five studies of [[time-of-use-tariff|time-of-use tariffs]] for households.
Run once, on data the author cleaned by hand in a spreadsheet.
Peak demand fell 6.2 kW per pump.
study.label: The co-op, its farms and every number here are fictional: the results are assumed example outputs, not computed from data.

forms.title: The review form
lines: 1. The study in one or two sentences: question, method, data.
2. The main claim it will make, and the evidence it plans.
3. Major concerns (at most three): ones that could change the conclusion. For each: the rubric competence, and what evidence or change would answer it.
4. Minor concerns.
5. One alternative method from another family, and what it would show that this one cannot.
6. Can the main result be rerun from the repository? What is missing?
7. Recommendation: proceed; proceed once the major concerns are answered; or rethink the question.

forms.title: The response
lines: For each concern, in the reviewer's order:
Concern 1 (competence): accepted / partly accepted / declined.
Reason: one or two sentences.
Change: what changed, and where (a section of the proposal, a file in the repository).
Evidence: a test, a figure or a number, where you have one.

forms.title: The change log
lines: One line per change:
Before → after · the concern it answers · where.
Then: your rubric self-rating after the revision, competence by competence, and any level that moved, with its evidence.

forms.title: The rerun report
lines: Repository and commit; date; machine and environment.
Tolerance for the main result, written down before the rerun.
Reported value; rerun value; difference as a share of the reported value (in the result's units if that value is near zero).
Qualitative work: the audit trail followed from the raw material, each theme traced to its sources, coding decisions and discrepancies explained.
Cause of any difference, and the fix in the repository.
Who reran it (you, or someone else).

tasks.title: Your review of the co-op proposal
tasks.freezeNote: Submitted: your review stays as you wrote it, before the marked tasks. Tick the points it makes below.
tasks.prompt: Review the co-op proposal above with the review form: the study in one or two sentences, at most three major concerns, the minor ones, and what would answer each. Paste your review.
points: The study summarized fairly in one or two sentences (question, method, data) before any criticism.
Major concerns (those that could change the conclusion) kept apart from minor ones.
Each major concern tied to a rubric competence by name.
For each major concern, the evidence or change that would answer it.
tasks.solution: Your own review. Tick the points it makes; the worked review of this proposal, with notes, opens in the Worked solution section once all twelve tasks are answered.

tasks.title: The most serious concern
tasks.prompt: Which concern could most change the study's conclusion?
options: Only five studies are cited, all of households, so the map of what is known is thin.
Each farm chose whether to join, so the joiners may differ from the rest in ways that also change their pumping.
The proposal does not name the software, or its version, that ran the regression.
The board votes on the tariff in 2026, which leaves the study little time to finish.

why.a: A real gap in Positioning: farm studies might show a factor the proposal misses. It needs checking, but threatens the causal claim less directly than selection.
why.b: Farms that could shift easily (a storage pond, pump timers) may have joined first, and their demand might have moved differently anyway: [[selection-bias|selection]] could produce much of the fall.
why.c: Worth a line in the methods, since versions can change results; it threatens the conclusion less directly than selection.
why.d: A constraint on the study, not a flaw in its conclusion.

tasks.solution: Joiners chose the tariff, so their demand might have moved differently even without it ([[selection-bias|selection bias]]). Different starting levels alone do no harm: [[parallel-trends|parallel trends]] needs evidence. The other three need checking too, but threaten this causal claim less directly.

tasks.title: Whose peak?
tasks.prompt: A reviewer writes: “The proposal never says whose peak: each pump's own highest hour, or the co-op's highest-load hours.” Which rubric competence does this concern?

why.a: Framing's Proficient level asks for a metric with units; “peak demand” names neither the hours nor whose peak.
why.b: Positioning is about the literature and the gap.
why.c: Integrity is about licences, credit, conflicts and the people a study affects.
why.d: Communication is about how results are shown; this is about what is measured.

tasks.solution: Framing: a metric with units. The board pays for the co-op's highest-load hours ([[coincident-peak|coincident peak]]), so the pumps' average kW in the co-op's 20 highest-load summer hours answers its question; each pump's own peak does not.

tasks.title: Answering the selection concern
tasks.prompt: The authors answer the selection concern. Which response answers it, rather than deflecting it?
options: Self-selection affects most observational studies, so we list it as an accepted limitation in section 6.
We will add more pumps from this summer to the sample, so that the estimate is more precise.
We now compare the 2024 joiners with the 29 farms that joined in 2025, before they joined, and show both groups' four summers before the tariff.
The reviewer has misunderstood the tariff: farms join it for reasons that have nothing to do with pumping.

why.a: It names the problem and keeps it: no change, no evidence.
why.b: More pumps of the same kind keep the same selection, however precise the estimate.
why.c: Another comparison group (farms that also chose to join), and the summers before as evidence that the groups' demand moved alike: [[parallel-trends|parallel trends]].
why.d: A claim about why farms join, with no evidence for it.

tasks.solution: Answer with a change and evidence. The 2025 joiners are one possible comparison; their four summers before 2024 test whether the two groups' demand moved alike ([[parallel-trends|parallel trends]]), which matters more than equal starting levels.

tasks.title: From Proficient to Strong
tasks.skill: Move a competence up a level
tasks.prompt: The revised study is Proficient on Method fit: difference-in-differences, defended against a matched comparison and a pump-scheduling simulation. Which change moves it to Strong?
options: Add a third alternative method, an agent-based model of the farmers, to the methods compared.

State the method's main limit here (the later joiners' demand might still have moved differently) and partly mitigate it: show that both groups' peak-hour demand moved together in the four summers before 2024.
Replace difference-in-differences with a machine-learning model trained on every pump's hourly readings.
Write a longer method section that explains difference-in-differences step by step.

why.a: More alternatives repeat the Proficient move.
why.b: Method fit's Strong level asks for the chosen method's limits, stated and partly mitigated.
why.c: A different method, with limits of its own; not a stated limit of this one.

tasks.solution: Method fit's Strong level: “limits of the chosen method stated and partly mitigated”. Limit: the later joiners' demand might still have moved differently. Mitigation: the two groups moved together, within 0.5 kW a year, in the four summers before 2024.

tasks.title: Your mock review
tasks.prompt: Get a written review of your research capstone's question and method (the review form; a mentor, a peer, or you after a day away). Paste it, and say who wrote it.
points: The reviewer named by role: a mentor, a peer, or you after a day away, with the form.
Each major concern tied to a rubric competence by name; if the reviewer found none, what they checked.
Your method tested against an alternative from another method family.
Each major concern says what evidence or change would answer it.
tasks.solution: Your own review. A reviewer other than you catches what you cannot see; a self-review with the form, after a pause, still finds most gaps in framing and method.

tasks.title: Your response
tasks.prompt: Answer each major concern point by point: accepted, partly accepted or declined, with a reason, and for each accepted one the change and where it is made. Paste your response.
points: Every major concern answered: accepted, partly accepted or declined, each with a reason.
Each accepted concern names its change and where it is made (a section, a file).
Each change matches its concern: a concern about the analysis or the method changes them, not only the wording.
Any declined concern answered with evidence or a stated limit, not an assertion (tick it if you declined none).
tasks.solution: Your own response. The worked response to the co-op study's selection concern shows a change, its place and new evidence.

tasks.title: Your revision
tasks.prompt: Revise your proposal. Paste your change log (before → after, and the concern each change answers) and your rubric self-rating after the revision.
points: A change log: each change as before → after, with the concern it answers.
The revised question still passes the question card's eight checks.
The rubric self-rating redone after the revision, competence by competence.
Each competence that moved up shown with its evidence; if none could (one already Strong, say), the log says why.
tasks.solution: Your own revision. The worked revision of the co-op study shows what moved it from Proficient to Strong.

tasks.title: A clean-clone rerun
tasks.prompt: After the review, the authors rerun the revised co-op study from a clean clone. Each step needs the one before it. Put the steps in order.
items: Clone the repository into a new, empty folder.
Build the environment from the repository's lock file.
Fetch the raw data with the repository's script, which runs in that environment, and check the checksums.
Run the whole pipeline, from raw data to the main result, with one command.
Compare the main result with the reported value, against the tolerance written down beforehand.
Log the outcome, and any difference with its cause, in the verification log.
tasks.solution: Clone, environment, data, run, compare, log. The download script runs in the environment, so the environment comes first; each step uses only what the repository holds, so a missing file or a hand step shows up.

tasks.title: How far apart?
tasks.prompt: Reported: a fall of 4.6 kW per pump. The clean-clone rerun: 4.3 kW. How far apart are they, as a share of the reported value?

unitNote.kW: kW gives the gap's size; the task asks for it as a share of the reported value.

tasks.tolNote: Within 2% of the value (about 0.13 percentage points) counts as right.
tasks.solution: (4.6 − 4.3) ÷ 4.6 = 0.3 ÷ 4.6 = 0.065, or 6.5% of the reported value: far over the 1% tolerance written down before the rerun.

tasks.title: What to report
tasks.prompt: The tolerance written down before the rerun was 1%. What should the authors do?
options: Report 4.6 kW, the published value: a gap of 0.3 kW is small next to the interval.
Report 4.3 kW instead, since the clean clone is the run to trust, and drop 4.6.
Find the cause, turn any hand step into code with a stated rule, rerun from a clean clone, and log both numbers, the cause and the fix.
Widen the tolerance to 10%, since 1% was too strict for real meter data.

why.a: 6.5% is far over the 1% set beforehand: until the cause is known, neither number can be trusted.
why.b: The rerun may be the wrong one; a quiet swap hides the problem.
why.c: A difference beyond the tolerance is a finding: explain it, fix it in the repository, and say so.
why.d: Moving the tolerance after seeing the result defeats it.

tasks.solution: Here the cause was three pumps whose meters were replaced mid-summer, removed by hand under a rule the data note set before any result. The rule is now in the cleaning script; the rerun gives 4.6 kW, and the log says so.

tasks.title: Your rerun
tasks.prompt: Rerun your own main result from a clean clone, or follow your audit trail for qualitative work. Paste your rerun report (the form above).
points: A new, empty folder and the environment built from the repository's own files; or the audit trail followed from the raw material.
A tolerance written down before the rerun; for qualitative work, what would count as the same finding.
Both values and the difference: as a share of the reported value, or in the result's units when that value is zero or near it; or each theme traced to its sources.
Any difference explained and its cause fixed in the repository (or none found), logged in the verification log; coding decisions documented.
tasks.solution: Your own rerun. Someone else rerunning it from your repository is the Strong level of Trustworthy analysis.

revision.title: The revision: what moved it from Proficient to Strong
revision.task: The revised study's question, method, checks and result.
revision.note: Illustrative: the study is fictional, and its results are assumed example outputs, not computed.

answers.label: Revised: Proficient

parts.text: Did the 2024 tariff lower the joining pumps' average demand in the co-op's 20 highest-load summer hours, compared with farms that joined in 2025, before they joined?
parts.note: Typed, with an audience (the board), a metric with units and a counterfactual.

parts.text: difference-in-differences, defended against a matched comparison and a pump-scheduling simulation.
parts.note: Two alternatives, one from another family (simulation).

parts.text: reruns from a clean clone within 1%; a verification log; the pumps' summed readings checked against the meters of the feeders that serve only pumps, same hours, after line losses.
parts.note: A clean-clone rerun, a log and one check against an independent reference ([[feeder|feeder]] meters): of the measurements, not of the tariff's effect.

parts: Result: 4.6 kW per pump (95% interval 2.9 to 6.3).

answers.label: Revised: Strong

parts.text: and is the fall above 1.5 kW per pump, the least for which the board would keep the tariff?
parts.note: Framing's Strong level: the answer that would change the decision.

parts.text: Limit: the later joiners' demand might still have moved differently. Mitigated: in the four summers before 2024 the two groups moved together, within 0.5 kW a year.
parts.note: Method fit's Strong level: the method's limit stated and partly mitigated.

parts.text: a co-op engineer reran the clean clone and got 4.6 kW.
parts.note: Trustworthy analysis at Strong, first half: reproduced by someone else.

parts.text: summer 2025, not used to build the analysis: the same code on the 29 farms that joined in 2025, against the 42 that never joined.
parts.note: Second half: data not used to build it, a named comparison group, and a rule written down before looking.

parts.text: the check supports the main estimate if its whole 95% interval is above 1.5 kW, so the board's decision would not change. 2025: 4.1 kW (1.8 to 6.4): it is.
parts.note: Compatible with 4.6 kW, not proof the effects are equal; the two estimates share farms (the 29 were comparison farms before), so no interval for their gap is given. The never-joiners' demand may also have moved differently.

parts: Result: 4.6 kW per pump (95% interval 2.9 to 6.3), above 1.5 kW across the interval.

criteria.label: The review
levels: No review.
Comments on wording or format, or concerns with no competence and nothing that would answer them.
Major concerns (those that could change the conclusion), each tied to a competence and to the evidence that would answer it; the method tested against another family.
Also written by someone else, and ranked by what each concern could change in the conclusion.

criteria.label: The response
levels: No response.
Thanks and promises with no change, or concerns declined without reasons.
Every concern answered with a reason; each accepted one names its change and where; a concern about the analysis answered in the analysis.
Also new evidence for the changes (a test, a figure), and the reviewer credited.

criteria.label: The revision
levels: No revision.
Wording changed, the analysis not.
A before → after log; the question still passes the card's eight checks; the rubric self-rating redone.
Also each competence that moved up shown with its evidence, or, where none could, why.

criteria.label: The rerun
levels: No rerun.
Rerun in the working folder, not a clean clone, or a difference not reported.
A clean clone (or a complete audit trail), a tolerance set first, both values and the difference reported, any cause fixed.
Also rerun by someone else from the repository, within the tolerance.

rubric.look: After the revision your question card passes its eight checks, and your response says what answer would change your audience's decision.
Your response defends the method against the reviewer's alternative from another family, and states one limit you mitigated.
Your clean-clone rerun matches within the tolerance you set first, or the difference and its cause are in your verification log.
